stt: Ask HN: Best business advice for software developers
x:
I was a software engineer for 10 years (first 10 engs at LinkedIn -> first 10,000 at Google -> first 10 at Factual). After that I was about to start a company but fell into venture capital instead. Here are a few things I've learned about business from the VC side that I didn't appreciate very much when I was an engineer:

1) Customers don't care about the technologies you're using, the elegance of your XYZ algorithm, or the novelty of feature ABC. What they care about is solving some problem they have, making their day easier, becoming more productive, etc. When you're pitching your product, talk about how it helps the customer, not about how it's built. A great 5-minute video on this is "Understanding the Job" by Clayton Christensen: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f84LymEs67Y

2) Think about monetization early on. Like most engineers, I had dozens of side project and business ideas. For each idea, I had thought about the features I'd build and how I'd build them, but not the business viability: who would I sell to? What would the pricing model be? How much money would that translate to for a typical user? Would users have the work/personal budgets to pay what I wanted to charge? Was the price enough to cover marketing and user acquisition costs? I haven't read it, but have heard that a great book on this topic is Monetizing Innovation (https://www.amazon.com/dp/B01F4DYY1I). Another good book to think about business models is The Art of Profitability (https://www.amazon.com/dp/B000FA5TTM, brief notes: https://codingvc.com/the-art-of-profitability)

3) Finally, think about marketing and customer acquisition in parallel with product. After almost 5 years as a VC, I can readily confirm that most products don't sell themselves. Even the really good products need sales, marketing, etc. A great book to get started on marketing is Traction by Gabriel Weinberg (of DuckDuckGo) and Justin Mares (https://www.amazon.com/gp/aw/d/B00TY3ZOMS/)

stt: An ARM-based MacBook SE could destroy Chromebooks and mid-priced Windows laptops
x:
BUSINESS concepts behind the scenes:

a) What people don't understand about the SE strategy, besides economies of scale and a smaller, more powerful phone, is that the device was made to offer extreme value targeting a demographic using a specific strategy called "Price skimming": https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Price_skimming

The iPhone SE was designed to lower consumer's (Android users) barrier to entry (price) into the brand, to quickly gain market share, then sell them services or premium devices in the future. This is possible because of Apple's established reputation as a premium brand (as opposed to penetration pricing): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penetration_pricing

b) The "1st mover advantage" is a myth. Consider Facebook or Google, they gained near monopoly market share because they were first in their technology/approach, not market.

The 'Apple way' is to wait for competitors to test new markets and get consumer validation, lowering risks by learning from early competitor errors, then grab market share with a product that delivers a better UX due to its superior combination of technologies. Look at Fitbit's demise with the Apple Watch - Google is now trying to replicate its Android success by acquiring Fitbit- "2nd mover advantage" works if done right.

c) If a and b work, this will make no difference to users, considering that Apple's strategy will not be focused on apps (this is a strength in phones, not laptops), but rather to sell a value performance device for the general public.

The Macbook failed not because it targeted the wrong demographic (business users) vs Air (students and commoners) and Pro (other professionals), but because it failed to provide value as an 'entry level' device: low specs, highly priced - they (partly) wrongly assumed business users' willingness to pay a premium for portability (inelastic demand) without regard for the value.

Nevertheless, the Macbook offer (a 1st gen. test product) did serve its purpose by anchoring users to see the next better offer at hand- the Air. This strategy called "bundling" in 3 options: good (price), better (quality), best (both) often serves to guide users to avoid extremes by choosing the middle option (usually most profitable), also called the "center stage effect": https://kenthendricks.com/center-stage-effect/

I recommend reading Stanford consultants' "Monetizing Innovation" to understand these strategies: https://www.amazon.com/Monetizing-Innovation-Companies-Desig...

In sh

One of the biggest lessons I've learned as a VC in the past few years is that pricing really has to be aligned with and proportional to the value your product provides. If someone gets $100 of value per seat and you charge $15/seat, that's great. If you charge $15/seat for a product that creates value per gigabyte, people start gaming the system. E.g. they'll buy one seat for their company and ask that person to be the proxy user for your product. Or if you charge $10/GB and people get $20/GB of value of the first few gigabytes and then $5/GB of value after that, you're going to run into problems.

So figure out how users perceive and quantify your value to themselves, and then try to come up with a simple pricing scheme that captures 10-25% of that value. That way every time someone pays you $1, they get $4-$10 of value, and that's a no brainer purchase.

Getting pricing right has a huge ROI across the board. Good pricing improves margins, reduces sales friction, and creates happier customers.

The best book that I've read on pricing is Monetizing Innovation: https://www.amazon.com/Monetizing-Innovation-Companies-Desig...

stt: Ask HN: How to Price a Product
x:
The book Monetizing Innovation, to me, has been the smartest approach to pricing I've encountered: https://www.amazon.com/Monetizing-Innovation-Companies-Desig...

Basic idea is that you should design the product around the price. Do price discovery before you do anything else.

Podcast ep here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A6veeCbKIzw
